Chapter 1 · Trading Lingo

Reading the Shorthand

Traders don't talk in full sentences — they talk in code. The good news: it's not random. It's a small set of rules that, once you see them, you can read for life.

This chapter covers the exact reference-level and moving-average notation used on real trading charts — the kind of shorthand you'd see scribbled in someone's trading notes.
1

Key price levels

These are the levels traders watch before anything else — places price has already reacted to, so it might react there again.

The pattern

P+ D or W+ H, L, or C = Previous [Day/Week]'s [High/Low/Close]

Once you know this formula, you can decode PDH, PDL, PDC, PWH, PWL, and PWC without ever memorizing them individually.

Watch the exception: PMH and PML break the pattern. The "PM" here doesn't mean "previous month" — it means premarket, the session before the regular market opens. Same letters, different rule.
PDHTap
Previous Day High

What's the ceiling price hit yesterday?

The highest price a stock traded at during the entire previous trading day.

PDLTap
Previous Day Low

What's the floor price hit yesterday?

The lowest price a stock traded at during the entire previous trading day.

PDCTap
Previous Day Close

Where did it end yesterday?

The final traded price when the market closed on the previous trading day.

PMHTap
Premarket High

Trading starts before the opening bell — how high did it get?

The highest price reached today during premarket hours, before the regular session opens.

PMLTap
Premarket Low

And how low did it dip before the bell?

The lowest price reached today during premarket hours, before the regular session opens.

PWHTap
Previous Week High

Zoom out — what was last week's ceiling?

The highest price traded at any point during the previous full trading week.

PWLTap
Previous Week Low

And last week's floor?

The lowest price traded at any point during the previous full trading week.

PWCTap
Previous Week Close

Where did the week finish?

The final traded price at the close of the previous trading week (typically Friday's close).

2

Chart overlays

Tools traders draw or plot directly on the chart to see trend and volatility at a glance.

LRCTap
Linear Regression Channel

Is there a way to draw the "average direction" of price automatically?

A statistically-fitted trend line through recent price, with two parallel lines above and below it forming a channel — showing the trend and how far price has stretched from it.

BBTap
Bollinger Band

How do you measure whether the market is calm or chaotic right now?

A moving average with two bands plotted around it based on volatility. The bands widen when price swings get bigger and squeeze tight when things go quiet.

MTFTap
MTF Band (Ripster Cloud)

Can you see the "big picture" trend while zoomed into a small timeframe chart?

A higher-timeframe moving average pair plotted as a colored cloud on a lower-timeframe chart. On the 10m Ripster charts: green = daily 20/21 EMA band, blue = daily 50/55 EMA band.

3

Crack the moving average code

This is the deepest piece of lingo in this chapter — once you understand the grammar, you can read any moving average shorthand you'll ever come across.

The formula

Timeframe+ Period+ s or e

Timeframe — which chart you're looking at. Period — how many candles get averaged together. s / e — simple average or exponential average.

daily50s
The 50-period Simple Moving Average, plotted on the daily chart.
5m5s5 SMA on the 5-minute chart
hourly 5s5 SMA on the hourly chart
weekly 200s200 SMA on the weekly chart
5m325s325 SMA on the 5-minute chart
10m5/12e5 & 12 EMA cloud on the 10m chart (Ripster-style)
3.5

Setting Up Your Indicators

Here's what a real indicator panel looks like once it's built out — then a step-by-step for adding these on TradingView and Robinhood Legend.

Reference Panel

SMA 5 through 325, EMA 9 through 377, LinReg, and Bollinger Bands — all in one indicator list

This is the exact set of moving averages behind the shorthand grammar above — the same "timeframe + period + type" code, just applied across every period at once on a single chart.

Adding an SMA — TradingView

1

Open Indicators

With a chart open, click the "Indicators" button (the fx icon) in the top toolbar.

2

Search and select

Type "Moving Average" in the search box. Choose "Moving Average" for an SMA, or "Moving Average Exponential" for an EMA.

3

Open its settings

Hover over the indicator's name in the top-left of the chart and click the gear icon that appears.

4

Set the period

Change "Length" to the period you want (5, 20, 50, 200, etc.) and confirm "Source" is set to Close. Adjust the color/style so it's easy to tell apart from your other MAs.

5

Repeat for each MA

Go back to Indicators and repeat for every SMA/EMA you want stacked on the chart — this is how the full reference panel above gets built.

Adding an SMA — Robinhood Legend

1

Open a chart widget

From a stock's detail page, or any chart widget in your Legend layout.

2

Open the indicator menu

Select the indicator icon in the upper-right corner of the chart widget.

3

Find and add SMA

Search for "Simple moving average (SMA)" in the menu and select it to add it to your chart.

4

Set the period

Adjust the length/period directly in the indicator menu.

5

Save it as a set

Once you've stacked all the MAs you want, click the folder icon at the top of the indicator menu to save them as a named set — then apply that whole set to any other chart in one click instead of rebuilding it each time.

4

Quick check

Two questions. One has a trap in it.

What does PMH stand for?

"daily 50s" refers to which moving average?

Chapter · The 7 Rules

Making Money vs. Making Consistent Money

Anyone can win a trade. The traders who last are the ones who turned winning into a process — a set of rules that hold up on the boring days and the brutal ones alike.

"These aren't suggestions. They're the difference between a good month and a career."

1

The 7 rules

Tap any rule to open it up.

1

Road to $100,000 by 2027

The north star — every other rule serves this one

Why this matters

A number and a deadline turn trading from a hobby into a project. Without one, "doing well" is whatever feels good in the moment. With one, every decision gets a real question behind it: does this move me toward the number, or is it just noise?

Loading...
2

NEVER look at PnL while in a trade

Your plan was made with a clear head — protect it

Why this matters

You built your entry, stop, and target before emotion was involved. The second you're staring at a green or red number ticking in real time, you're reacting to a feeling, not executing the plan.

You're in a trade. It ticks up $80. Your thumb wants to open the PnL tab. Per Rule 2?

3

Emotion = Loss — step away to save the day

"Stop with the greed — $1,000 a day is a fantastic day"

Why this matters

Greed after a win is just as dangerous as fear after a loss. Naming a concrete "great day" number gives you a finish line — without one, there's always a reason to take "one more" trade.

It's 11am. You're already up $1,000. A tempting setup pops up. What does Rule 3 say?

4

GTFO: Get the F*ck out

2 losses = step back and live to fight another day

Why this matters

Two losses in a row is a signal you're misreading the day or yourself — a third trade to "win it back" is usually the worst one. If the setup you expect just isn't there, forcing it doesn't summon it into existence.

You've taken 2 losses today. Something fast-moving catches your eye and FOMO kicks in. Per Rule 4?

5

SWINGS: Size small, check all charts

Swings should be shares only, no options

Why this matters

A swing trade sleeps overnight, exposed to news and gaps you can't react to. That risk gets managed with smaller size and shares instead of options, so you're not stacking leverage on top of overnight risk.

You want to hold overnight and you're deciding between shares or a call option. Per Rule 5?

6

Journal every trade

Grade it A+ to C-, study why you took it

Why this matters

Grading forces honesty — an A+ trade can still lose money if the process was right, and a C- trade can still win despite bad process. That distinction is the entire game.

A+
A
A-
B+
B
B-
C+
C
C-
7

The Final Step: DON'T QUIT

Remember why you do this

Why this matters

Consistency isn't built by never having a bad week — it's built by not walking away when it gets hard. This closes the loop back to Rule 1: the goal you set is what pulls you back to the process instead of quitting on it.

Chapter 3 · The Mentor's Method

Reading Structure Like a Pro

A full walkthrough of how the mentor actually approaches the market — from the first chart pulled up in the morning to the account math behind every position. Real setups, real trades, real numbers.

1. Framework 2. Confluence 3. Levels 4. Macro Setups 5. Execution 6. Management 7. Toolkit 8. Account & Sizing 9. Quick Reference
1

The Daily Framework

Before anything else, every day starts by figuring out what kind of day it's going to be — and setting up the charts to actually see it.

Premium day vs. cash-flow day

A premium day is defined by macro-level breaks — the big, high-conviction moves. A cash-flow day is smaller, built from remounts, rejections, and sneaky hourly pivots. Knowing which kind of day it is shapes what setups to even be looking for.

The four-window setup

Charts are run as a synced, split four-window view: hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly, all moving together. Monthly and weekly are the starting point — especially for swing analysis — to get the big picture of where price has been. Daily and hourly are the primary tools for day trades.

The Real Windows

One of the regular four-window charts — this one with a daily panel

And a synced four-window view running 1h / 1D / 1W / 1M together on a ratio chart, right alongside the watchlist:

The 1-minute chart isn't part of this. Nothing lower than a 5-minute chart gets used. Multi-timeframe analysis is what shows the full picture of where price has been and where it can go — a single low timeframe can't do that on its own.
2

Confluence & Relative Strength

The setup gets stronger when multiple things line up at once — across timeframes, and against the broader market.

What confluence looks like

Confluence is supply/demand zones lining up on multiple timeframes and lining up with the general market being traded against (QQQ). If a stock is approaching a remount level at the same time QQQ is approaching one too, that's a much higher-conviction bounce than either alone.

QQQ stays up on screen at all times as that benchmark — here it is run across 1D / 1h / 5m together:

NVDA — Relative Strength

Barely sells off when QQQ dips. The read: buy the dips into demand.

TSLA — Relative Weakness

Barely moves up when QQQ rips. The read: stay sell-biased, short the pops into supply.

"Always check for relative strength and weakness intraday, based on the first 30 minutes to an hour of the day — this changes over time."
When the market rests, we rest. Trading only happens where there's value. Chasing a trade off its level changes the reward-to-risk for the worse — there is always another entry: a remount, a rejection, a second entry, or a sneaky hourly pivot.
3

Finding the Levels

Before a trade can happen, there has to be a level worth trading. Here's how those levels get found.

Congestion = the level

Areas where price has congested on higher timeframes (monthly, weekly, daily, hourly) mark the key zones of potential supply and demand.

Moving averages define the zone

A set of moving averages across those same higher timeframes is used to pinpoint exact levels of supply/demand, and to gauge the measured potential (MP) of a trade — how far it could realistically run.

Where VWAP fits

VWAP only gets used on smaller timeframes, like the 5-minute chart. The exception is anchored VWAP — anchored from an all-time high or low — which can be an important level on its own regardless of timeframe.

4

Macro Setups — The Big Moves

Macro setups are the trades to focus on first when building an account — lower frequency, but the highest conviction and measured potential.

The two macro patterns

1) A clean break of the 50-day or 200-day SMA. 2) A stock consolidating for days or weeks in a tight range, then breaking that range — especially when the range break coincides with the 50 or 200 SMA.

Case Study — META Macro Breakout

A full walkthrough from consolidation to confirmed pivot to the options execution

1

The setup

META spent over a month consolidating in a tight daily range below the 50-day SMA. Almost no supply existed above the SMA except the daily upper Bollinger Band — meaning very little stood between price and a real move if it broke.

2

The level

On the weekly chart, the high from the past month sat at 482.5.

3

The confirmation — why 482.5 was the macro pivot

482.5 confirmed three things at once: the top of the daily range, the top of the weekly range, and the 50-day SMA. That stacking is what makes a level a genuine macro pivot rather than just a number on a chart. A build above it meant several days to weeks of higher prices could be expected, with clear runway (next weekly supply wasn't until over 500) — the kind of clear-blue-sky setup that's ideal for options.

4

The move

After confirming 482.5, META rode the daily 5 SMA higher every single day, then began basing above 500.

5

The options play

Traded with shares directly (PDT-exempt), but for a smaller account building leverage: slightly out-of-the-money calls, at least 1–2 weeks to expiry so a multi-day runner can actually be held. The key technique — the same indicators get applied to the option contract's own price chart, not just the underlying stock.

ContractMETA 500c, 6/14 exp
Contract LOD$3.35
Entry (contract's daily 10 SMA)$3.45 ($345 BP)
Next-day high$10.80 ($1,080)

Profit-taking was based on both the underlying (META hitting supply zones) and the contract's own supply zones — the contract's daily 20 SMA/EMAs, then the upper Bollinger Band the following day.

5

Execution Techniques

Once a level is identified, how it actually gets traded depends on the stock's personality and which entry type applies.

Liquid names (AMZN, AAPL)

Leave a resting bid at the level, stop 50¢–$1 below.

Fast / spready names (NFLX, pre-split NVDA)

Wait for the break, then remount: buy back above the level once it reclaims, using the wick low after the break as the stop. A rejection is the same idea shorting at supply.

The second entry

Pivot breaks, makes a new high/low, retraces 30–60¢, then continues. The second entry is right at that first new high/low after the break — safer, because it confirms real buyers or sellers are there, though it doesn't always happen (especially on macro breaks). First entry gets taken on macro breaks with more size; second entry gets taken on continuation moves.

Ex.

Pivot at 500 → breaks, new high of 501, retraces to 500.30 → second entry is 501 with a 70¢ stop at 500.30.

The hourly sneaky pivot

A level gets tested multiple times across several hourly candles before finally breaking — similar to a "flat top breakout." Pre-split NVDA topped out at exactly 1199.99 on several hourly candles before breaking 1200; the entry used the previous hourly candle's low (1195) as the stop, and NVDA ran to 1250 that same day — $50 of reward on $5 of risk per share.

Harmonics — used loosely, not by the textbook

Harmonic patterns (XABCD-style) get used too, but the ratios rarely land exactly on the textbook numbers in practice. A W-shaped harmonic generally leans toward a sell bias at point D; an M-shape leans toward a bounce. Even when the pattern suggests a reversal at a prior all-time-high retest, that doesn't necessarily mean expecting a new low — it can simply be an added spot to take profit or raise stops, not a standalone signal to fade the move.

Patterns as structure, not memorization

Classic patterns (bull/bear flags, head and shoulders, etc.) are recognized and add confluence, but execution is primarily off moving-average reclaims/rejections. The real lens is candle psychology — long wicks showing who's trapped and who's in control — and a favorite edge is trading a failed pattern: when a bullish or bearish setup fails, a fast move often follows in the opposite direction.

An inverse head-and-shoulders isn't really a pattern to memorize — it's just structure changing from lower-highs/lower-lows to higher-highs/higher-lows. Thinking in structure and who's stopping out where removes the need to memorize pattern names at all.

Case Study — NVDA Failed Head & Shoulders

Pre-split, ~400 level

1

The setup that looked bearish

A large bearish engulfing candle at the all-time high, followed by a retest and failure (double-top feel), then a full head-and-shoulders pattern that broke its neckline at the 400 level. Many traders shorted that breakdown.

2

The failure — and what followed

The daily candle closed green and reclaimed the 400 psychological level — a clean head-and-shoulders breakdown failure. That failure led to a fast retracement and an epic run from 400 to nearly 1000 before any major dip.

Case Study — TSLA MTF Breakdown

Friday 6/5/26 — 10m chart, 5/12e clouds, daily-level MTF bands

1

The break

TSLA lost the daily 20e and 50e, shown on a 10-minute chart carrying 5/12e Ripster clouds plus MTF bands pulling in daily levels (green = daily 20e, blue = daily 50e) — two charts in one.

2

The entry sequence

Each valid entry used the previous 10-minute candle's high as risk (a 5-minute candle can be used for a more aggressive, slightly higher-probability-of-stopout version):

1

Rejection of the daily 20e (green MTF band)

2

Bounce back up into the 10m 5/12e cloud

3

Loss of the daily 50e (blue MTF band)

4–6

Repeated bounces back into the 10m cloud

The further an entry sits from the original break, the more likely price eventually bounces back and reclaims the cloud — so entries beyond these were skipped. The best trade stayed in until the cloud finally reclaimed, which didn't happen until late in the day. These same arrow points double as add-back locations if scaled out along the way down.

6

Trade Management

Getting in is half the job. This is how a trade gets sized, tracked, and closed out.

Never guess the close. The only goal is to win the interval intraday. The only thing held overnight is a runner from an earlier move — unless the trade was built as a swing from the start.

PDH / PDL as targets

A stock can't go higher without taking out its previous day high, and can't go lower without taking out its previous day low — so these levels double as scale-out targets. If a stock (or the market) isn't taking out PDH or PDL, it's an inside day: low value. Inside days can be scalped at the range extremes with equity, but options bleed premium too fast to be tradeable on days like that.

Stop sizing

Most setups carry roughly a $1 initial stop. More advanced/aggressive sizing risks to the previous 5-minute or hourly candle's high/low on high-probability, large-measured-potential setups like macro breakouts. Swings risk to the previous daily candle's high/low.

Scaling out and managing the balance

Rather than exiting all at once, profit gets taken in pieces at each supply/demand level on the way, with the goal of holding a small piece for the full measured potential. Once scaling begins, the stop on the remainder typically moves to break-even — meaning every trade resolves as either a small loss, a break-even/small gain, or a large gain on the piece held for full MP. Positions are never scaled into on losers — it's right, or right out.

Reading the tape

Level 2 and time-and-sales ("the tape") show how a stock actually builds above or below a pivot — large orders sitting at key levels, liquidity getting swept. Each stock develops its own personality over repeated screen time, which is what eventually makes the whole process feel calm rather than reactive.

Example below: AAPL building below the key 212 level — waves of red prints on the bid, showing price is more likely to keep going lower.

"If you ever get nervous while trading, you're in a bad trade — many times from being oversized or simply not following the rules of the strategy."

Consider the other side

Every trade gets weighed against the other side of the market: where are opposing longs or shorts stopping out, what is everyone else seeing on this chart. It won't produce a 100% win rate — that's what trade management and psychology are for.

7

Indicators & Toolkit

The specific indicators used to confirm setups and find levels beyond raw price action.

BX-Trender

"B-Xtrender @Puppytherapy" by QuantTherapy

A MACD + RSI blend showing money flowing in and out of a stock. Used mainly as a second layer of confirmation, particularly for swing trades.

Market Bias Indicator

Custom settings, moving-average style

Plots similarly to a moving average and is used as a directional bias reference alongside BX-Trender.

VPOC

"THT Volume Pro" by tradinghelpingtraders

The red line marking volume point of control — a key volume-based level layered on top of price structure.

Ripster Clouds (10m 5/12e & 34/50e)

TradingView, default settings

Used to buy dips on aggressively trending names when the hourly level is too far away. BIRD is a strong example — each time it consolidates and the 10m cloud catches up, the next leg starts.

MTF Horizontal Bands

Daily EMAs overlaid on the 10m chart

Green = daily 20e/21e band, blue = daily 50e/55e band. Lets the 10m chart show the daily trend without switching timeframes — dips hold these as support, or they act as supply to scale out into.

8

Account Structure & Position Sizing

How the accounts themselves are organized, and the actual math behind a real day-trade position.

Separate accounts by purpose

Day trading, swing trading, and long-term/IRA capital are kept in separate accounts for organization. PnL only gets checked monthly — profits are withdrawn and the account resets, keeping the focus on execution quality rather than the daily number.

Leveraged shares vs. regular shares

Leveraged shares work best in a cash account — in margin, selling them doesn't replenish buying power until the next day. Regular shares work best in a margin account (typically 4x buying power on cash), where selling replenishes buying power same-day. One exception: Lightspeed provides time-and-tick on margin even for leveraged shares, so those get traded intraday there for maximum leverage — except when shorting a hard-to-borrow name.

Broker choices

Lightspeed — direct market access, fast execution, paid per trade; primary for equity day trading. Fidelity — excellent fills, no payment-for-order-flow, but no overnight access. Schwab/TOS — overnight (BLUE) access. Bull/Hood are fine options depending on where someone is in their journey, though not primary accounts here.

Day trades vs. swings — entry approach

Day trades: a single entry, margin/leverage for size, no averaging in — right or right out. Swings: up to three scaled entries (e.g. 250 / 250 / 500 shares toward a 1,000-share goal, heaviest on the lowest entry), targeting general chart areas rather than penny-precise levels, since focus is split across multiple swing positions and accounts. If a pullback holds a trend line or moving average, averaging up into it is still typically cheaper than buying full size on the first dip.

Position Sizing Walkthrough — TSLA

100k margin account example

Account size$100,000
Buying power (4x on cash)$400,000
Entry — dip buy / rejection500 shares
Risk per share$1–2 (~$1k max w/ slippage)
Scale-out400 shares sold, locked ~$3k
Runner held overnight100 shares (~$40k in securities)
Next-day BP (4x cash + 2x securities)~$332,000
Gap-up exit next morning+$1k more, total trade value $4k+

Risk generally stays at 0.5%–2% of the account on any stop-out. Bounces and rejections stay on the lighter end (~0.5%); a genuine macro-level pivot or a tight daily-50-SMA reclaim is worth sizing up toward full buying power, since these are the account-building moves that make a quarter or a year.

Chapter 4 · Weekly Watchlist

What's On Deck

A running log of the stocks actually being watched, why, and at what levels — sent in raw and organized here into something clean enough to actually reference during the week.

1

How this works

This chapter updates continuously rather than once — new tickers get added as they come in.

Send it in raw

A ticker, the reason it's on the radar, and any key levels being watched — however rough. Chart screenshots help but aren't required. Each one gets turned into a clean card below, organized by the week it was added.

On the "different every week, sometimes days" part

No fixed cadence needed — that would fight how you actually trade. The approach: send names whenever a name earns a spot, no matter how often that is. When a new batch comes in, whatever's currently in "This Week" that hasn't been touched in a while slides down into Archive automatically, so the page always shows what's actually active without you having to manage two lists by hand. If a name stays hot for three weeks straight, it just stays in "This Week" — nothing forces it out on a timer.

What's useful to include per name
1

Ticker — the name itself

2

The why — what's actually interesting about it right now (a level, a setup forming, relative strength/weakness, news, whatever the actual reason is)

3

Key levels — the specific prices being watched (pivot, support/resistance, whatever applies)

4

Status — watching, triggered, or passed on, once that becomes relevant

What happened: MU dropped roughly 7% intraday, from Friday's close of $966.78 down into the high $800s/low $900s, on the same day AMD and SNDK also sold off. No MU-specific news — this is a broad semiconductor pullback, with the market de-risking ahead of NVDA's earnings Wednesday and PCE/GDP data. MU's own next earnings report isn't until late September — no company-specific catalyst here at all.

Reading the Timeframes

Start wide, per the four-window framework, before zooming into what today's drop actually means.

Monthly / Weekly — the big picture

MU is up over 200% year-to-date and sits 64% above its 200-day SMA ($571.10). This is still a strong, intact long-term uptrend by any measure — a 7% single-day drop doesn't come close to threatening that structure. This is exactly the distinction the mentor's framework is built around: don't let a daily-chart move override what the higher timeframes are actually showing.

Daily — where today's drop actually lands

Before today, MU was already sitting 2.8% below its 50-day SMA (~$964.59) — meaning this pullback started before Monday, not because of it. Today's drop pushes price down toward the 20-day SMA (~$896.24), which was acting as support heading into the session. Whether that level holds is the entire question this chart is asking right now.

3

The Levels That Matter

Real moving averages, not rounded estimates — this is what "finding the levels" looks like with actual numbers.

20-Day SMA — ~$896

Today's immediate battleground. A close back above this on strong volume would be the first sign of stabilization. A clean break below opens room toward the 100-day.

50-Day SMA — ~$965

The level price had already lost before today. A reclaim of this would be the real macro signal — the kind of level the Mentor's Method chapter builds entire trades around.

100-Day SMA — ~$808

Well below current price — the next real demand zone if the 20-day fails to hold. Still 100%+ above the 200-day, so even a move here doesn't break the long-term trend.

200-Day SMA — ~$571

The line that actually defines the long-term trend. Price is nowhere near it — a useful reminder of how much room a "scary" daily drop can have before it means anything structurally.

Confluence Check

Is this MU's problem, or the market's? This is the relative-strength/weakness read from Chapter 2 of The Mentor's Method, applied live.

Sector-wide, not company-specific

AMD and SNDK sold off the same morning, with Nasdaq futures down broadly. That's the tell: this isn't a MU-specific read-through, it's a semiconductor sector de-risking move ahead of NVDA's earnings and same-day PCE/GDP data. No MU news, no earnings this week. When a stock drops in lockstep with its sector on a macro-driven day, that's a fundamentally different situation than a stock dropping alone on its own bad news — same red candle, very different meaning.

Tomorrow, MU opens and reclaims the 20-day SMA (~$896) in the first 30 minutes, holding above it into the close. Per the framework, what does that tell you?
